pages.title: Bedtime Story Coloring Book Prompts for Calm Evenings
pages.metaDescription: Five 24-page bedtime story coloring books, written page by page: a badger's lost blanket, a city walk, a sleeper train, a lighthouse cat, a dream sheep.
pages.intro: A bedtime story coloring book gives the last half hour of the day a shape: color a page, read its line or two, turn to the next. Here are five bedtime stories of 24 pages each for ages 3 to 13, from a badger cub hunting for his blanket and a girl's goodnight walk around the block to a sleeper train, a lighthouse cat and a dream ride with the hundredth sheep. Each book is written out page by page, with the picture and the words for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Twenty-four pages is a gentle bedtime read; color three or four pages a night and the book lasts a week.
Give the story a clock (dusk, lamps on, moonrise, bed) so each run of pages sits later in the evening.
Selling several on KDP? Keep each book's hero and setting distinct, like these five, so the titles don't compete.

prompts.name: Bramble the badger cub's lost blanket

fields.title: Where Is Bramble's Blanket?
fields.description: A 24-page bedtime story. Bramble, a badger cub with a white stripe and pajamas too big for him, cannot find his patchwork blanket at bedtime. He searches the twilight wood: under the ferns, at the rabbits' burrow, the frog pond, the owl's oak, the hedgehogs' leaf pile, the squirrels' nest, the fireflies' meadow and the old stone wall where the moths sleep. Each friend points him onward. In a hollow log he finds the blanket, now a nest for five baby mice. He shares it, they all fall asleep, and Mama Badger finds them under the moon.

prompts.why: Parents of toddlers get a full 24-page goodnight story that visits one sleepy animal home after another and ends with the hero asleep.
prompts.pageStyle: Black-and-white story coloring page for a child aged 3 to 6. Bramble is a small round badger cub with a white stripe down his face and baggy striped pajamas with rolled-up sleeves; his blanket is a patchwork of squares. Thick bold outlines, big simple shapes, little background, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a plain blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.
pages: Bramble the badger cub standing at the round door of his burrow under a big oak tree at sunset, yawning wide, his long pajama sleeves flopping over his paws.
Bramble in his little bedroom inside the burrow, staring at his empty moss bed with his paws on his cheeks, a pillow and a tiny lamp but no blanket anywhere.

Bramble at the rabbits' burrow in a grassy bank, a mother rabbit tucking three bunnies into a row of tiny beds and pointing a paw down the path.
Bramble trotting along a winding woodland path, holding up the too-long legs of his pajamas, mushrooms and a fallen pine cone beside the path.
Bramble at the edge of the frog pond, three frogs on round lily pads with their mouths open in a goodnight song, cattails along the bank.
A big frog on a stone in the pond pointing toward a huge oak tree, Bramble beside him on the bank, a dragonfly asleep on a reed.
Bramble at the bottom of the owl's big oak looking up, a round owl in a nightcap leaning out of a hole in the trunk, a crescent moon behind the branches.
Bramble watching four little hedgehogs curl up into balls in a cozy pile of autumn leaves, a mother hedgehog patting the leaves smooth.
A squirrel family snuggled in a round nest of twigs high in a tree, Bramble waving up at them from the roots, a pile of acorns at his feet.
Bramble at the edge of a meadow full of tall grass and daisies, dozens of fireflies drawn as little glowing dots floating around him.
Bramble following a line of fireflies across a little wooden bridge over a stream, holding the rail, a fish jumping in the water below.
Bramble at an old mossy stone wall where big soft moths sleep in the cracks, one moth fluttering down to land on his nose.
A moth with patterned wings pointing its feeler at a hollow log lying in the ferns, Bramble tiptoeing toward it with his paw raised.
Bramble spotting a corner of his patchwork blanket poking out of the end of the hollow log, his eyes wide and his mouth open in surprise.
Bramble kneeling and peeking into the hollow log, five baby mice snuggled together on his patchwork blanket like a nest, one tiny mouse waving.
A mother mouse standing on the log beside her babies, holding her paws together, Bramble listening with his head tilted, an acorn cap cup beside her.
Bramble sitting on the ground with his paws on his knees, thinking, the hollow log beside him and the baby mice peeking out at him.
Bramble smiling and crawling into the big hollow log on his hands and knees, the five baby mice making room for him on the blanket.
Inside the log, Bramble lying on his side with the patchwork blanket pulled over him and all five baby mice tucked under it with their ears showing.
Mama Badger walking through the dark wood carrying a lantern on a pole, peering ahead, a sleepy owl watching her from a branch.
Mama Badger kneeling at the end of the hollow log, smiling at Bramble and the mice asleep inside, her lantern set down on a flat stone.
The hollow log in a little clearing under a big round moon and stars, Mama Badger lying curled beside it, the ferns and mushrooms quiet all around.
Bramble fast asleep and smiling, filling the page, the patchwork blanket up to his chin and a baby mouse asleep on his paw, a few stars around them.
pageTexts: The sun was going down over the wood, and Bramble the badger cub gave a great big yawn.
It was bedtime, but his patchwork blanket was not on his bed. "Where is my blanket?" said Bramble.
He looked under the ferns. No blanket there, just a ladybird fast asleep.
He asked Mother Rabbit. "We haven't seen it," she said. "Ask the frogs at the pond."
So Bramble set off down the path, holding up his too-long pajamas.
The frogs were singing their goodnight song. "Ribbit, goodnight! Ribbit, sleep tight!"
"No blanket here," said Big Frog. "Ask the owl in the old oak."
Owl was just waking up. "I go to work at night," said Owl, "but I have not seen a blanket. Try the hedgehogs."
The hedgehogs were curling up in their leaves. "No blanket in here," they yawned.
High in the tree, the squirrels called down, "Follow the fireflies! They see everything."
In the meadow, the fireflies lit up one by one, like tiny lamps.
They led Bramble over the little bridge, blink, blink, blink.
At the old stone wall, a soft moth landed on his nose. "I know where it is," she whispered.
"Look in the hollow log," said the moth. Bramble tiptoed closer.
There it was! A corner of his patchwork blanket, poking out of the log.
Bramble peeked inside. Five baby mice were snuggled up on his blanket, warm and cozy.
"I'm sorry," said Mother Mouse. "My babies were so cold tonight."
Bramble sat down and thought. It was his blanket. But the mice were so small.
"There is room for everyone," said Bramble, and he crawled inside.
He pulled the blanket over himself and all five baby mice. It was the coziest bed in the wood.
Back home, Mama Badger took her lantern and went looking for Bramble.
She found him in the hollow log, fast asleep with his new friends. She smiled.
Mama Badger curled up beside the log, and the big moon kept watch over them all.
Goodnight, Bramble. Goodnight, little mice. Goodnight, wood.

prompts.name: Noor's goodnight walk around the block

fields.title: Goodnight, Noor's Street
fields.description: A 24-page bedtime story. Noor, a five-year-old with two puffs of curly hair and star-print pajamas under her coat, takes an evening walk around the block with her dad. They pass the baker closing his shutter, the florist bringing in buckets, the grocer's crates, the bus driver ending her last route, pigeons on the bridge rail, the park being locked, a window cat, the night nurse heading to work and the streetlights coming on one by one. Back home come bath, teeth, pajamas, a story with Dad and a last wave to the Moon before she sleeps.

pageTexts: After dinner, Dad zipped Noor's coat right over her star pajamas. "Time for our goodnight walk," he said.
Down the front steps they went, hand in hand, out into the evening street.
Mr. Hamid the baker was pulling down his shutter. "Goodnight, Noor! Fresh bread tomorrow!"
The florist was carrying her flowers inside. Noor held the door for the sunflowers.
At the corner shop, the grocer stacked his crates up high. One apple sat on top like a hat.
The bus came to its very last stop. The driver stretched her arms. Her day was done.
On the bridge, the pigeons tucked their heads under their wings. Goodnight, pigeons.
At the park, the swings were empty. The park keeper locked the gate. Goodnight, park.
Three dogs trotted home for supper. The smallest one sniffed Noor's boots to say goodnight.
A sleepy cat watched from her window. Noor waved, and the cat blinked slowly back.
A nurse walked past on her way to work. "Some people work while we sleep," said Dad.
Click, click, click! The streetlights came on, one after another, all down the street.
From up on Dad's shoulders, Noor saw the Moon rise between the buildings.
Then it was home again, up the stairs. Noor counted every step.
Splish, splash! Noor had a warm bubble bath with her little boat.
Dad dried her curly hair with the fluffiest towel. It tickled!
Brush, brush, brush. Top teeth, bottom teeth, all clean.
On went the star pajamas again, and Ellie the elephant waited on the bed.
Noor chose one story from the shelf. Just one, because it was late.
Dad read the story, and Noor's eyes grew heavy.
Noor knelt at the window. "Goodnight, Moon. Goodnight, street."
Down below, the shops were dark and the street was quiet.
Dad turned on the little moon light. "Goodnight, Noor," he whispered.
And Noor was fast asleep, with Ellie in her arms and the Moon in her window.

prompts.name: Theo's overnight sleeper train

fields.title: The Night Train to Grandma's
fields.description: A 24-page bedtime story. Theo, seven, red-haired and holding a stuffed rabbit called Parsnip, rides the overnight sleeper train with his mom to his grandma's house in the mountains. He finds his little cabin, eats soup in the dining car, watches fields and a sunset, meets the conductor with her brass lantern, sees a sleeping town glide past, climbs into the top bunk, counts tunnel lights, spots deer by a moonlit lake and drifts off as the train climbs. He wakes at dawn to snowy peaks, and Grandma is waiting on the platform with a thermos of cocoa.

prompts.why: Grandparents and parents of early readers get a 24-page bedtime journey with a new view on almost every page and a reunion at the end.
prompts.pageStyle: Black-and-white story coloring page for a child aged 6 to 9. Theo is a seven-year-old boy with messy hair, freckles and a striped sweater or pajamas, with Parsnip, a stuffed rabbit with one floppy ear. Clean medium outlines, moderate detail, simple background, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a plain blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.

The conductor kneeling in the narrow corridor to show Theo her brass lantern up close, its little flame behind the glass, Parsnip peeking over his arm.

An owl sitting on a wooden fence post beside the track, its eyes wide as the train goes by, a farmhouse with one light far behind it.

The conductor walking softly down the dark corridor at midnight with her brass lantern, the cabin doors closed on both sides.
The long train winding up into the mountains in the moonlight, the track curving around a cliff and tall pine trees below.

The train pulling into a small mountain station with a wooden roof and snow on the platform, a sign post and a bench, smoke rising from a chimney.

pageTexts: The big station clock said seven o'clock. Theo held his mom's hand and stared at the long night train.
The conductor held up her brass lantern. "Tickets, please! And who is this?" "This is Parsnip," said Theo.
Their cabin was tiny, with two bunks, a sink and a window. Theo bounced on the bed. It was perfect.
He unpacked his toothbrush, his flashlight and his pajamas, and gave Parsnip the top pillow.
With a jolt and a whistle, the train began to move. Theo waved until the station was gone.
Back gardens rushed by: washing lines, sheds and a boy on a fence who waved back.
Then came the fields, gold and wide, and the sun sank down behind the hills.
In the dining car, they ate warm soup with crusty rolls while the world went by.
At a crossing, a farmer on a tractor waited for them. Ding, ding, ding went the bell.
A little town slid past, sleepy and still, with only a few lights left on.
The conductor let Theo look at her lantern. "It has lit the way on this train for forty years," she said.
Brushing your teeth on a train is tricky. The whole cabin swayed, and Theo giggled.
Up the ladder he climbed to the top bunk, with Parsnip under his arm.
Whoosh! Into a tunnel. Theo counted the lights. Ten, eleven, twelve...
Out by a lake, two deer lifted their heads as the train went by in the moonlight.
The train rumbled over a tall stone bridge, high above a river far below.
Mom read a chapter from his book. Theo listened, and his eyes grew heavy.
An owl on a fence post watched the train go by. Hoo, hoo, goodnight.
Clickety-clack, clickety-clack. The train rocked Theo gently to sleep.
At midnight, the conductor walked softly down the corridor with her lantern. All was well.
All night long, the train climbed up and up into the mountains.
In the morning, Theo pulled up the blind. Snow! Mountains everywhere, pink in the sunrise.
The train slowed and stopped at a little snowy station.
And there was Grandma, with a big hug and a thermos of hot cocoa. "You made it!"

prompts.name: Marigold the lighthouse cat

fields.title: Marigold Keeps the Light
fields.description: A 24-page bedtime story. Marigold, an orange cat with one white paw, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky island with the keeper, Mr. Penrose. Every evening she climbs the 99 spiral steps to watch him light the lamp, then follows the beam across the sea. Tonight it sweeps over fishing boats heading in, seals on the rocks, the late ferry, puffins in their burrows, a sailboat with a torn sail that the beam guides into the harbor, a whale and leaping dolphins, and the village going dark window by window. When every boat is tied up, Marigold curls up on the keeper's armchair and sleeps.

Clean medium outlines, moderate detail, simple sea background, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a plain blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.

pageTexts: On a rocky island far out at sea lived Marigold, an orange cat with one white paw, and Mr. Penrose, the lighthouse keeper.
Every evening began the same way: fish for Marigold and a pot of tea for Mr. Penrose.
Then up they went, ninety-nine spiral steps. Marigold always got to the top first.
Mr. Penrose polished the great glass lens until it shone. Marigold watched a hundred little cats look back at her.
He struck a long match, and the lamp burst into light. The night's work had begun.
Marigold sat on the railing and followed the beam as it swept round and round across the sea.
The beam found the fishing boats coming home, with full nets and hungry gulls behind them.
It passed over the seals on the rocks. A little pup blinked up at the light.
The late ferry crossed the bay, its windows glowing like a string of beads.
On the cliff, the puffins were going to bed in their burrows, one with a last fishy snack.
Then the wind picked up and the waves grew tall. Mr. Penrose lifted his binoculars. "Look, Marigold. Someone's out there."
A little sailboat was tossing on the waves, its sail torn, its sailor all alone.
Round came the beam, and it shone a bright path straight across the water. "Follow the light!" Marigold seemed to say.
The sailboat followed the beam all the way into the harbor, safe and sound.
Later, when the sea was calm again, a whale rose up in the moonlight and blew a great spout.
Two dolphins leaped right through the beam, as if they were playing in it.
Across the bay, the village went to sleep, one window at a time.
The last fisherman tied up his boat and walked home with his lantern. Every boat was in.
Mr. Penrose wrote it all in the logbook. Marigold helped by lying on the page.
"Good work tonight, Marigold," he said, and gave her a sardine.
Then Marigold padded back down the ninety-nine steps, much more slowly this time.
Her favorite chair was waiting by the warm stove.
She curled up, and Mr. Penrose tucked the blanket around her. "Goodnight, little keeper."
And the light kept turning all night long, over a calm sea where every boat was safely home.

prompts.name: Ivy and the hundredth sheep

fields.title: The Hundredth Sheep
fields.description: A 24-page bedtime story. Ivy, ten, with a long braid and round glasses, can't fall asleep and starts counting sheep. The hundredth one, a sheep named Woolsey in a nightcap, stops, steps into her room and offers her a ride on a cloud. They float over the sleeping town to the dream islands: a library with pillow shelves, a night bakery making moon-shaped rolls, a river of warm milk with paper boats, an observatory where owls polish the stars, a garden of glowing night flowers and a hammock field. As the sky turns grey, Woolsey tucks Ivy back into bed, and she is asleep before he leaves.

prompts.why: Parents of older kids who resist bedtime get a 24-page dream adventure with real places to color and a story that ends back in bed.
prompts.pageStyle: Black-and-white story coloring page for a child aged 9 to 13. Ivy is a ten-year-old girl with a long single braid, round glasses and striped pajamas; Woolsey is a big fluffy sheep in a long nightcap with a tassel. Fine clean outlines, detailed scenes with full backgrounds to color, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a plain blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.

pageTexts: It was way past bedtime, and Ivy was wide awake. The clock ticked. The Moon stared in. Sleep would not come.
"Fine," Ivy sighed. "I'll count sheep." One sheep jumped the fence. Then two. Then three.
Ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine... but sheep number one hundred did not jump. He stopped right on top of the fence and looked at her.
Then he stepped down onto her bedroom rug. "Good evening," said the sheep. "I'm Woolsey. You seem to be having trouble sleeping."
Woolsey opened the window. A cloud was waiting there, soft as a pillow. "Shall we go for a ride?"
Ivy pulled on her dressing gown and slippers and climbed out onto the cloud. It was like stepping into whipped cream.
They floated over the rooftops of her town. Everyone she knew was asleep down there.
They passed the clock tower just as it struck midnight, and the river shone silver below.
Then, ahead in the stars, Ivy saw them: the dream islands, floating in the sky and joined by little rope bridges.
The first island was a library where the shelves were made of pillows, so the books could rest too.
Ivy found a cozy nook and read. Around her, books flapped their pages and flew from shelf to shelf.
On the next island was a bakery that only opened at night. The mole baker made rolls shaped like the Moon.
Ivy and Woolsey shared a warm roll. It tasted like honey and sleepy Sunday mornings.
Beyond the bakery flowed a river of warm milk, carrying hundreds of tiny paper boats.
"Every boat is someone's wish for tomorrow," said Woolsey. Ivy folded one of her own and set it sailing.
On the highest island stood an observatory, where owls worked all night polishing the stars.
An owl handed Ivy a star and a cloth. She rubbed until it glowed, and the owl hung it back in the sky.
Through the great telescope, Ivy could see every crater on the Moon, close enough to touch.
In the night garden, flowers glowed softly, and moths drifted from bloom to bloom.
The last island was a field of hammocks. Woolsey flopped into one and pulled his nightcap over his eyes.
Ivy climbed into a hammock and gave an enormous yawn. "Time to go home," said Woolsey gently.
They floated back over the town as the sky turned grey at the edges. Morning was on its way.
Woolsey tucked Ivy into her own bed and smoothed the quilt. "Sleep well, Ivy."
She was asleep before he reached the window. In the morning, there was a tuft of wool on her pillow.

pageTexts: It was a big day. Hazel the hedgehog was starting preschool!
Hazel ate her berries and toast. Her tummy felt a little wobbly.
She packed her lunchbox, her spare socks and Beetle, her very best toy.
Mom tied a bright red bow on her quills. "Ready?" asked Mom.
They walked past the pond. The ducks said quack, quack, good morning.
There was Acorn Hill Preschool, under the great big oak tree.
Hazel hugged Mom tight. "I will come back at pickup," Mom said.
"Welcome, Hazel," said Mrs. Badger. "We are so glad you came."
Hazel found her very own cubby with an acorn on it. In went her backpack.
At circle time everyone sang a clapping song.
Hazel did not feel like singing yet. She held Beetle close.
Then it was painting time. Hazel painted a big yellow sun.
The mole next to her painted a worm. "I'm Dot," she said. "I like your sun."
Hazel and Dot built a tall, tall tower. Crash! They both giggled.
At snack time Dot spilled her berries. Hazel shared hers.
They washed their paws together. Bubbles, bubbles everywhere!
Mrs. Badger read a story about a little boat that was brave.
Then it was time to rest. Hazel and Dot had mats side by side.
Outside, Hazel filled buckets and Dot dug a long tunnel.
Whee! Hazel went down the slide, and Dot came right after.
Everyone helped tidy up. Hazel put the blocks away.
There was Mom at the gate! Hazel ran to show her the sun painting.
"I made a friend," said Hazel. "Her name is Dot."
That night Hazel smiled in bed. Tomorrow she would sit with Dot again.

pageTexts: Mateo woke up early. Today was his first day of kindergarten!
He put on his new sneakers. Stomp, stomp! They lit up with every step.
Abuela made pancakes, his favorite. "For a big kindergarten boy," she said.
Mateo zipped up his dinosaur backpack. It was almost bigger than him.
He held Abuela's hand all the way down the street.
At the corner the crossing guard held up her sign. Mateo gave her a high five.
All the kindergartners lined up by the big red door.
"Good morning, Mateo," said his teacher. "I'm Ms. Okafor."
Mateo hung his backpack on his very own hook.
Everyone sat on the big rug. Mateo put his hand up to say hello.
At show-and-tell Mateo held up Stego. "He has plates on his back," he said.
The class went to the library. Mateo found a book full of dinosaurs.
Later Mateo went to the bathroom and washed his hands all by himself.
But on the way back, every door looked the same. Where was his class?
A big girl stopped. "Are you lost? Your room is right down there."
Mateo was back! A boy named Ben waved at him from his table.
At lunch the cafeteria was big and loud. Mateo held his tray tight.
Abuela had put a heart in his lunchbox. Ben sat right next to him.
At recess they played tag. Mateo's sneakers flashed as he ran.
Mateo and Ben swung as high as the sky.
In art Mateo painted the biggest dinosaur he could.
At the end of the day everyone helped put the chairs up. "See you tomorrow!"
There was Abuela at the gate! Mateo ran to her as fast as he could.
All the way home Mateo told Abuela everything. "Can I go back tomorrow?"

pageTexts: Priya's new bedroom was full of boxes. Out the window, Willow Creek looked very quiet after the city.
"First day at a new school," said Mom, brushing her ponytail. Priya's stomach did a flip.
At the bus stop there was no subway, just a long road and a field of corn. Then the yellow bus came.
Priya sat by herself and watched the barns and cows go by. Everyone else seemed to know each other.
The bus stopped at Willow Creek Elementary. A huge willow tree stood by the front door.
In the office a kind woman gave Priya a paper with her room number on it.
Priya opened the first door she found. It was full of kindergartners! Wrong room.
The next door was right. "You must be Priya," said Mr. Hale. "Welcome to third grade."
"This is Rosa," said Mr. Hale. "She will be your class buddy today." Rosa waved hard.
Rosa showed Priya her desk. "I put a star on it for you," she said.
"Want to feed Mr. Slow?" asked Rosa. Priya had never fed a snail before.
In science they used magnets. Priya's paper clips made the longest chain in the class.
In math Mr. Hale asked Priya to draw a pattern on the board. She got it right.
Lunch was outside under the big oak tree. Rosa traded Priya a cookie for a grape.
"What are your patches?" asked Rosa. Priya told her all about the city.
At recess the class played soccer. Priya scored a goal!
"You're really fast," said Rosa, puffing. Priya grinned.
After lunch the class worked in the school garden. Priya watered the tomatoes.
Priya pulled up a carrot as long as her arm. Everyone laughed.
After school there was comic club in the library. "Come with me," said Rosa.
Priya drew a comic about a new girl and a snail. Rosa said it was the best one.
When the bell rang, Priya and Rosa hugged by the buses. "See you tomorrow!"
On the bus home Priya drew a map of her new school, so she would never get lost again.
"This is my classroom, and this is where Rosa and I eat lunch," Priya said. Willow Creek felt like home.

pageTexts: Gloop was starting first grade at Mossy Bog Monster School. Mom packed his favourite lunch: mud pies.
Gloop wiggled his one wobbly tooth. What if the other monsters were bigger and scarier than him?
The school bus was a giant caterpillar. It crawled up to the stop on a hundred wiggly legs.
Gloop sat between a monster with one huge eye and a monster with curly tentacles. Bump, bump, bump!
Mossy Bog Monster School was a swamp full of hollow tree stumps, each one a classroom.
Gloop's classroom was inside the biggest stump of all. The desks were toadstools!
"Good morning, little monsters," boomed Professor Grizzle. "I am your teacher."
First was roaring class. Everyone roared ROAR! Gloop opened his mouth and went... squeak.
Gloop felt silly. Then a fluffy monster tapped his shoulder. "I'm Fern. I like your squeak."
Next was puddle-jumping. Gloop and Fern made the biggest splash in the whole bog.
In cave painting Gloop pressed his hand on the wall. Now everyone would know he was there.
In counting class they counted fireflies in a jar. Gloop counted twelve. Fern counted thirteen.
At lunch Gloop and Fern shared mud pies. Gloopy, gloppy, delicious!
Crunch! Gloop's wobbly tooth popped right out into his mud pie. "You lost a tooth!" cried Fern.
At recess they went down the slime slide. Squelch! Whoosh!
Then they swung on the vines, higher and higher over the moss.
Professor Grizzle counted to ten for hide-and-seek. All the little monsters ran.
Gloop was small, so he hid under a bucket. Nobody could find him at all.
"Gloop wins!" called Professor Grizzle. Being small was good for something after all.
In music class Gloop played the bone xylophone. Plink, plonk, plink!
The music made Gloop feel brave. He took a deep breath and ROARED. Professor Grizzle gave him a gold star.
At the end of the day the caterpillar bus was waiting. Gloop held Fern's hand.
Gloop and Fern rode home side by side, waving to the frogs in the reeds.
"I lost a tooth, I found a roar and I made a friend," said Gloop. "Monster school is the best."

Jonah in the right science lab, taking a stool at a black lab bench beside Ana, beakers, test tubes and safety goggles in front of them.
Jonah and Ana in safety goggles leaning back as a baking-soda volcano fizzes and foams over the top of a flask on their lab bench.
Jonah at his desk in math class chewing the end of his pencil over a surprise quiz sheet, the teacher walking between the rows.
A packed hallway between classes, Jonah squeezing through a crowd of taller students with his planner held tight, a big wall clock above.
Jonah standing in a huge, loud cafeteria holding a lunch tray, long tables full of laughing students and no empty seat in sight.
Ana waving Jonah over to her table, where two other sixth graders slide over to make room on the bench.
Jonah in the quiet school library at the end of lunch, sitting in a beanbag reading a graphic novel, tall shelves and a librarian at her desk.
Band class: Jonah holding a clarinet to his mouth with puffed cheeks, music stands in a half circle and a band teacher wincing at a squeak.
Gym class: Jonah running laps around an outdoor track with his class, a coach with a whistle and clipboard calling out from the side.
Social studies: Jonah and his classmates gathered around a big globe on the teacher's desk, a wall map and posters of mountains behind.
The final bell: students flooding out of classroom doors into the hallway, backpacks swinging, Jonah heading toward the lockers.
Jonah opening his locker on the very first try, the door swinging wide, a triumphant grin on his face and Ana giving him a thumbs-up.
Jonah and Ana at the bike rack after school, Jonah unlocking his bike while Ana waves before walking off with her friends.

pageTexts: The night before sixth grade, Jonah practiced his locker combination over and over. Right, left, right. It never opened the same way twice.
He lay awake thinking about seven classes, a building twice the size of his old school and a locker that might never open.
In the morning Dad handed him his lunch. "Middle school," Dad said. "You've got this."
Jonah rode his bike to Ridgeview Middle School, wind in his messy hair and butterflies in his stomach.
The bike rack was jammed. Everybody looked older, taller and like they knew exactly where to go.
In the gym a teacher handed him his schedule. Seven classes, seven rooms, and only four minutes between them.
Then came locker 214. Jonah spun the dial three times. Nothing. He tried again. Still nothing.
An eighth grader stopped. "Lift the handle while you turn the last number," he said. Click! It opened.
Jonah found Room 108 and walked in. A whole room of eighth graders stared at him. Wrong lab.
The right lab was next door. His lab partner was a girl named Ana. "I got lost too," she whispered.
Their first experiment was a fizzing volcano. It foamed all over the bench, and they both cracked up.
In math the teacher said, "Pop quiz, just to see what you know." Jonah took a deep breath and did his best.
The hallways were a river of people. Jonah held his planner like a map and made it to every class on time.
Then came lunch. The cafeteria was so loud Jonah could barely think, and every seat seemed taken.
"Jonah! Over here!" It was Ana. Her friends slid over to make room.
With ten minutes of lunch left, Jonah found the library. It was quiet and calm, his new favorite spot.
In band Jonah picked the clarinet. His first note came out as a squeak, and the whole row laughed with him.
In gym they ran laps. By the last one Jonah was tired, but he was still smiling.
In social studies they spun the globe and talked about places to explore this year.
Finally the last bell rang, and the whole school poured into the hallways at once.
Jonah walked up to his locker, lifted the handle and turned the dial. It opened on the very first try.
At the bike rack Ana waved. "See you in science, partner!"
At dinner Jonah told his family everything: the wrong lab, the volcano, the squeaky clarinet and his new friend.
That night he wrote in his planner: Day one, done. He couldn't wait for day two.

pageTexts: One spring morning, Mama and Papa had big news. "A baby is coming," said Mama, "and you are going to be a big sister."
Juniper pressed her floppy ear to Mama's tummy. She heard a tiny swish, swish.
The carrots in the garden grew and grew, and so did Mama's tummy.
At bedtime Juniper wondered about the baby. Would it hop? Would it play with her?
Papa painted the little room for the baby. Juniper helped paint orange carrots all along the wall.
Papa built a wooden cradle, and Juniper held the box of pegs.
In her toy box Juniper found her old baby rattle. "The baby can have this," she said.
Juniper sorted tiny socks into pairs. They were so small they fit on her paw!
Every evening Juniper read a story to the baby in Mama's tummy.
One night Mama said, "It is time!" Grandma Rabbit came hopping over to stay with Juniper.
Juniper and Grandma baked carrot muffins and waited for the telephone to ring.
In the morning Papa called. "Come and meet your baby brother!" Juniper picked daisies on the way.
There in Mama's arms was a tiny bunny with a pink nose. "This is Sprout," said Mama.
Juniper shook her old rattle very gently. Sprout opened one sleepy eye.
Sprout came home to the burrow. Juniper held the door open wide.
Sprout cried. He cried at breakfast, he cried at lunch, and he cried at bedtime too.
When Sprout slept, everyone whispered. Juniper could not bounce her ball at all.
Mama was busy with Sprout all day long. Juniper felt left out and a little sad.
Papa sat with her in the garden. "Sprout is lucky to have a big sister like you," he said.
One evening Sprout would not stop crying. Mama rocked and Papa hummed, but nothing worked.
Juniper leaned over the cradle and sang her carrot song: "Crunch, crunch, carrots in a row, sleepy little bunny, down you go."
Sprout stopped crying. He looked up at Juniper and gave a tiny yawn.
From then on, Juniper sang the carrot song to Sprout every single night.
"I am Sprout's big sister," said Juniper, "and I know just the song he likes."

Rosa counted on her fingers: one big sister and two baby brothers. Her family was growing fast.
Suddenly everything came in twos. Dad built two cribs while Rosa read out the instructions.
Two car seats filled the back of the car. Rosa squeezed into the middle and wondered where her knees would go.
Rosa folded two of every tiny hat, two of every sock and two of every sleepsuit.
Mom's tummy grew so big that Rosa measured it every Sunday with a tape measure.
Leo and Max were born on a rainy Tuesday. Rosa pressed her nose against the nursery window.
The twins looked exactly alike: the same round cheeks, the same tiny noses, the same wisps of hair.

pageTexts: Tumble woke up in the den and rubbed his eyes. A tiny new pup was curled up on Mama's tummy.
"This is your sister, Ripple," said Mama. Ripple sneezed right on Tumble's whiskers.
Ripple could not swim yet. She rode on Mama's tummy while Mama floated down the river.
When Ripple was bigger, she touched the water. "Too cold! Too wet!" she squeaked.
Tumble showed her how to float. "Lie back and look at the sky," he said.
Where the river ran fast, Tumble held Ripple's paw so the water could not pull them apart.
Next Tumble taught her to dive. Down they went, with bubbles trailing behind.
Under a stone Tumble found a crayfish. Ripple looked too, and found a pebble.
She tried again and again. At last Ripple caught a crayfish all by herself!
Then Tumble cracked a mussel on a flat stone, right on his tummy. Tap, tap, crack!
Ripple tried. The stone slipped and the mussel bonked her on the nose.
Ripple tried once more. Tap, tap, crack! She opened her very first mussel.
Then came the best lesson of all: sliding! Tumble whooshed down the muddy bank. Splash!
Ripple stood at the top of the slide. It looked very, very high.
"We'll go together," said Tumble. Whee! They slid down side by side.
After all that mud, Tumble showed Ripple how to comb her fur until it was fluffy.
A heron landed in the shallows. "Shh, let's hide," whispered Tumble, and they ducked into the reeds.
The heron flapped away over the trees. Ripple let out a big breath.
At nap time all the otters floated together, holding paws so no one drifted off.
Every day Ripple swam a little farther on her own.
One day Ripple looked across the river. "I want to swim to the far bank by myself," she said.

pageTexts: On a Saturday morning, Mom and Dad sat Eli down at the kitchen table. "We're going to adopt a baby," Mom said. Eli nearly dropped his camera.
First came the paperwork, a stack of forms as thick as a dictionary. Eli took a photo of it, just for proof.
Ms. Alvarez, the social worker, came to visit. She asked what kind of big brother Eli would be. "The kind who takes lots of pictures," he said.
That spring they turned the spare room into a nursery. Eli painted the walls with a roller taller than he was.
Dad put the crib together, and Eli hung a mobile of paper birds he had folded himself.
Then they waited. Months went by on the kitchen calendar, and every time the phone buzzed, everyone jumped.
Summer turned into fall. Some days Eli wondered if the baby would ever come.
Then, one snowy night at dinner, the phone rang. Mom listened, and her hand went to her mouth.
"A baby girl was born today," she said. "Her name is Ruby." The three of them hugged in the middle of the kitchen.
They packed in twenty minutes flat: the car seat, a suitcase, diapers and, of course, Eli's camera.
Ruby had been born in another state, so they drove through the night. Eli watched the highway lights until his eyes closed.
At sunrise they pulled up at the hospital, tired and nervous and excited all at once.
A nurse placed Ruby in Mom's arms. She had a full head of dark hair and the tiniest fingernails Eli had ever seen.
Then it was Eli's turn. He sat very still while Dad helped him hold his sister for the first time.
Eli took his first photo of the three of them. Then a nurse took one of all four.
They could not go home yet. For a week they lived in a hotel room, waiting for the adoption papers to be finished.
In that hotel room Eli learned to test a bottle on his wrist and to burp Ruby over his shoulder.
Every afternoon they pushed Ruby's stroller around the snowy park next to the hotel.
On the seventh day the papers were ready. Mom and Dad signed their names, and Eli gave a double thumbs-up.
They flew home. Ruby slept on Dad's chest the whole flight while Eli photographed the clouds.
At home the neighbors had hung a giant banner across the porch, and everyone came out to wave.
Grandma arrived with a quilt she had sewn all year, with a square for every person in the family.
That night Eli gave Ruby her first bath at home, with Dad holding her head and Eli holding the washcloth.
Eli glued every photo of the trip into an album. He called it The Day Ruby Came Home.

pageTexts: Trixie was the smallest triceratops in the herd. Every morning she splashed in the river while her mother drank beside her.
One afternoon a thunderstorm crashed over the valley. The herd ran for shelter, and Trixie hid under a big fern.
When the rain stopped, the valley was quiet. Trixie looked all around, but her herd was gone.
Trixie took a deep breath. "I will find them," she said, and she set off on her short, strong legs.
On a tall cliff sat a pteranodon. "Have you seen my herd?" Trixie called up.
"I saw big dinosaurs walking that way," said the pteranodon, and it pointed to the fern forest.
In the fern forest Trixie found footprints so big she could stand inside one. She followed them, step by step.
The footprints belonged to a kind brachiosaurus. "Your herd went toward the river," she said softly.
Stomp, stomp! The ground began to shake. Trixie hid behind a fallen log and kept very still.
A big T. rex wandered past, yawning a giant yawn. It never saw Trixie at all.
At last Trixie reached the river, but it was wide and fast. How could a little triceratops get across?
A diplodocus was wading nearby. "Hop on," it said, and it laid its long tail across the water like a bridge.
Trixie walked along the tail, one careful step at a time, all the way to the other side.
By now Trixie was very hungry. She found a bush full of juicy berries, just out of reach.
A parasaurolophus family pulled the berries down for her. "Share with us," they said, and they all ate together.
The baby parasaurolophus blew through its crest. Toot, toot! Trixie laughed so hard her frill wiggled.
Further on, smoke puffed from a far-off volcano. An ankylosaurus stood on the path. "Wait here with me until it clears," he said.
They sat under a rock ledge and told each other stories while the smoke drifted by.
Soon the sky was clear again. "Good luck, little one," said the ankylosaurus, and Trixie trotted on.
Trixie climbed a tall hill. It was steep, but she kept going, up and up and up.
From the top she could see the whole valley. And there, by the river, was her herd!
Trixie ran down the hill as fast as her legs could go.
Her mother saw her and came running. She nuzzled Trixie's nose and held her close.
The herd circled round, happy to have Trixie home. That night she slept safe and warm beside her mother.

pageTexts: Owen was hunting for a fishing net in Grandpa's shed when he found something strange: a big speckled egg in a bucket of straw.
He carried it to his room, wrapped it in socks and set it under his desk lamp to keep it warm.
Crack! Out popped a baby ankylosaurus with a bumpy back and a tiny club on the end of its tail.
"I'll call you Clunk," Owen whispered, because that was the sound his tail made on the floor.
Owen kept Clunk a secret. The first week he hid him in the laundry basket, right under Mom's nose.
Clunk grew fast. By the second week he only fit in the bathtub, and he loved the bubbles.
Soon the bathtub was too small, so Owen wheeled Clunk out to the yard in Grandpa's wheelbarrow.
For a few days Clunk lived in the treehouse, until he was too big to turn around.
Now Clunk was as big as a pony. Owen built him a tent from a tarp and brought him apples every day.
One morning Clunk ate every one of Grandpa's tomato plants. "Clunk!" groaned Owen.
The next day Clunk chased the mail truck all the way down the street. Letters flew everywhere.
Then he spotted the birdbath. Swing, smash! Clunk's tail was a lot stronger than it used to be.
Owen swept up the pieces. Clunk hung his head. "You can't help being a dinosaur," Owen sighed.
On Monday Owen walked to the school bus stop, and Clunk followed him there.
"Hide!" Owen said, pushing Clunk into the hedge. The bus driver scratched his head.
That night Owen read his dinosaur book to Clunk. Ankylosaurs lived in warm swamps, it said, long ago. Clunk looked homesick.
The next morning Grandpa lifted the tarp. He looked at Clunk. He looked at Owen. Then he started to smile.
"So that's where my egg went," said Grandpa. "Come with me. I have a secret too."
Behind the boxes was a door that glowed. Grandpa opened it, and warm air rushed in.
On the other side was a steamy swamp full of giant ferns and dragonflies as big as birds.
Out of the reeds came a family of ankylosaurs. Clunk lifted his head and gave a happy rumble.
Owen hugged Clunk goodbye. Clunk nudged a smooth round stone into his hand, like a present.
Back home, Owen put the stone beside the eggshell on Grandpa's shelf. "Can we visit him?" he asked. Grandpa winked.
That night Owen fell asleep with the stone in his hand, dreaming of a little dinosaur splashing in a faraway swamp.

pageTexts: High on a sea cliff lived a family of pteranodons. Wren, the smallest, had a crooked crest and wings that would not lift her.
One by one her brothers and sisters jumped off the ledge and soared away. Wren stayed behind.
Every day Wren practiced. Flap, flap, flap! But her feet never left the rock.
One windy morning she tried a big jump. Down, down, down she tumbled.
Splash! Wren landed in the sea. Then something big rose up underneath her.
It was a plesiosaur with a long, long neck. "Up you come," it said, and it carried her to a rock.
Wren spread her wings to dry in the sun. "Don't give up," called the plesiosaur as it swam away.
So Wren climbed all the way back up the cliff, claw over claw, ledge by ledge.
She stood at the edge, spread her wings wide and jumped. This time the wind caught her!
Wren was flying! She glided along the coast, looking down at the whole wide world.
She flew over a beach where duck-billed dinosaurs were sitting on their nests of eggs.
At the river mouth, a herd of triceratops looked up and waved their tails as she went by.
Wren was tired, so she rested on the head of a sauropod wading in a lagoon. It didn't mind at all.
On a sandbar a T. rex looked up and snapped its jaws. Wren flapped higher, far out of reach.
She flew past a smoking volcano island, where the air was warm and smelled of ash.
Then dark clouds rolled in. Rain lashed down and the wind pushed Wren this way and that.
Wren remembered the wind at the cliff. She found a rising draft of warm air and rode it up, up, up through the storm.
Above the clouds the sky was calm. Below her, the storm drifted away and a rainbow appeared.
Now Wren was hungry. Down below she spotted a shining school of fish.
She folded her wings and dove, straight as an arrow.
Splash! When she came up, a fish was wriggling in her beak. Her very first catch!
As the sun went down, Wren flew home along the coast with her fish.
Her family was waiting on the ledge. "You flew!" they cried, crowding around her.
The next morning, the whole family flew out over the sea together, and Wren, the smallest, led the way.

pageTexts: At the top of Fern Valley there was a bakery, and the baker was Bronte the brachiosaurus.
Bronte's oven was very high up, but her long neck reached it easily.
Today was little Stego's birthday, so Bronte mixed the biggest bowl of batter she had ever made.
She baked seven cake layers and stacked them up, one on top of another, into a volcano cake.
She drizzled frosting down the sides like lava and added candles on the top.
Bronte packed the cake into her wagon with bread, muffins, buns and pies, and off she went.
First she stopped at the farm. "A fresh loaf for the farmers!" The triceratops cheered.
Next came the ankylosaurus road crew, fixing the bumpy path. Bronte gave them warm muffins.
At the mail hut, the pteranodon mail carriers swooped down for sticky buns.
At the stream Bronte lifted the cake high on her head and stepped across, stone by stone.
By the lake, the duck-billed dinosaurs were having a picnic. Bronte brought them two big pies.
Then the sky grew dark. "Oh no," said Bronte. "Not rain, not today!"
Down came the rain. Bronte bent her long neck over the cake, but the rain kept coming.
Then a big T. rex stepped out of the trees and held a giant leaf over the cake. "I'll help," he said.
Together they walked through the rain, splashing in every puddle, and the cake stayed dry.
Soon the rain stopped and a rainbow came out. "Thank you!" Bronte called as the T. rex waved goodbye.
Bronte hurried on with the wagon. Stego's party was about to begin.
There was Stego's house, with balloons on the door and flags on the roof. Bronte was just in time!
Stego opened the door and gasped. "A volcano cake! For me?"
Bronte set the cake on the table, and all of Stego's friends gathered round.
Everyone from the valley came: the farmers, the road crew, the mail carriers, the picnickers and the kind T. rex. They all sang "Happy Birthday" to Stego.
Stego made a wish and blew out all the candles with one big puff.
Then everyone had a slice. It was the best cake in all of Fern Valley.
When the party was over, Bronte pulled her empty wagon home under the stars, happy and tired.

pageTexts: Sora was eleven the summer her aunt, a paleontologist, took her to a fossil dig in the badlands of Montana.
They set up camp between the striped hills, with tents, a camp stove and enough water for weeks.
Her aunt showed her the tools: rock hammers, brushes, dental picks and a notebook for writing down everything.
Each morning they hiked the dry gullies, eyes on the ground, looking for anything that was not just rock.
On the fourth day Sora spotted it: a round, weathered bone poking out of a hill. A vertebra!
Her aunt studied it through her lens and grinned. "This is a big one. Let's get the team."
First they mapped the site, with string and stakes, so every bone could be recorded exactly where it lay.
Then came the slow part: brushing away the rock, a little at a time, for days.
Slowly a giant hip bone appeared, wider than Sora's arms could reach.
Next came a leg bone. Sora lay down beside it. It was as long as she was.
At noon it was too hot to dig, so they ate lunch in the shade and guessed what the dinosaur might be.
Then, under a rock ledge, Sora brushed away the dust and found a horn. Then another, and another. It was a triceratops skull!
That night by the campfire, her aunt explained how triceratops lived here 66 million years ago, when this dry land was a green river plain.
In her tent Sora dreamed of the herd walking across a warm, green land, right where she was sleeping.
To move the bones safely, they wrapped each one in burlap soaked in plaster, like a cast for a broken arm.
One afternoon a hailstorm swept in. The team held a tarp over the jackets while hailstones bounced all around.
When it passed, the gully was running with muddy water, but every jacket was safe.
The skull jacket was too heavy to carry out, so a helicopter came and lifted it over the hills.
They loaded every jacket onto a flatbed truck, packed up camp and drove the bones to the museum.
In the museum lab, preparators spent months cleaning the bones, grain by grain, with tiny air-powered tools.
Sora came back to help on weekends, sorting small fragments and gluing broken pieces back together.
At last the skeleton was ready to stand. The team built a steel frame and raised it piece by piece.
On opening day, hundreds of people came to see the triceratops that Sora found.
Sora stood beneath it and read the sign: Discovered by Sora, age eleven. She was already planning next summer's dig.

pageTexts: Luna-Mae the mouse looked up at the big round Moon. "I think it is made of cheese," she said.
She could not stop wondering. There was only one way to find out for sure.
She found an old teapot, a silver thimble and two shiny spoons.
She tied on the spoons for fins and put the thimble on top. Her rocket was ready!
Luna-Mae put on her knitted helmet and packed a cracker for the trip.
She climbed in and counted down. Three, two, one...
Whoosh! The teapot rocket blasted off out of the window.
Up she flew, past the fluffy clouds and one very surprised bird.
She waved to a satellite turning slowly in the dark.
A sleepy comet gave a big yawn as she zoomed by.
Inside the rocket, Luna-Mae floated upside down. Her cracker crumbs floated too!
The Moon grew bigger and bigger. It was covered in round holes.

On the Moon she could jump so high! Boing, boing, boing!
She found giant old footprints. Someone had been here before!
Next to them was a parked moon buggy. She sat in the big seat and pretended to drive.
She dug in the dust with a spoon. It did not smell like cheese at all.
Then she saw Earth rising over the edge of the Moon. Home looked beautiful.
At last she licked a moon rock. Yuck! The Moon is not made of cheese.
Luna-Mae laughed, climbed back into her rocket and flew home.
Plop! She landed right in the sugar bowl.
For supper she had cheese on toast. Earth cheese is the best cheese of all.
That night the Moon shone in at her window, and Luna-Mae smiled in her sleep.

pageTexts: Kofi, eight, and his robot dog Bolt signed up for the Great Planet Rally: visit every planet, get a stamp at each and be the first one home.
On race day, rockets lined up on the school field. Kofi and Bolt climbed into theirs.
Three, two, one, go! The rockets roared up into the sky.
First stop was Mercury, closest to the Sun. It was so hot that Bolt's metal ears steamed.
A stamp robot stamped their card. One planet down, plenty more to go.
At Venus they dipped under thick, swirling clouds and spotted volcanoes far below.
On Mars a huge dust storm chased them across the rocks. Kofi steered as fast as he could.
They grabbed the Mars stamp beside a giant volcano just before the dust rolled in.
Next came the asteroid belt. Kofi zigzagged between the tumbling rocks.
A zippy saucer flown by a girl named Mira whizzed past. "See you at the finish!" she called.
Jupiter was enormous. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than the whole Earth.
A stamp drone met them beside Jupiter's moons. Stamp!
At Saturn, Kofi slid the rocket along the rings, past chunks of ice as big as houses.
Bolt leaned out on his safety line and caught a little ice chunk, like a game of fetch.
Uranus spins on its side. Kofi tipped his head to see it the right way up.
Neptune has the fastest winds of all. They shoved the rocket this way and that.
Then Bolt's battery ran out. The lights flickered and went dark.
Kofi found the backup pedal power and pedaled with all his might.
Bolt beeped back to life, and they got the last stamp at Neptune.
On the way home they waved to little Pluto with its heart-shaped plain.
They raced back toward Earth. Mira's saucer was just ahead.
Mira landed first. Kofi and Bolt came in second.
Then the judge checked the cards. Only Kofi's had a stamp from every planet.
Kofi and Bolt won the Explorer's Cup, and Mira asked if they could fly the rally together next year.

"Hello," said Ava. "Blip," said Blip, and waved all three antennae.
They showed Blip a cow. "Moo!" Blip jumped right up in the air.
In the chicken coop, a hen sat on Blip's head like a hat.
Grandma Rose gave them a bumpy ride on the big tractor.
They found a big muddy puddle. Splash! Blip loved puddles.
Sam picked Blip an apple off the tree. Crunch! Blip's eyes went wide.
The piglets snuffled Blip's toes, and he giggled and giggled.
They played hide and seek. Blip hid well, except for his antennae.
Before bed they lay on the grass, and Blip pointed to the tiny star that was his home.
At bath time Blip tried bubbles for the very first time.
At bedtime Grandma read a story, and Blip's antennae glowed like night-lights.
In the morning Blip looked at his broken ship and then at the sky. He wanted to go home.
"We can fix it," said Grandma Rose, and she fetched her toolbox, a colander and her sewing kit.
Sam and Blip fitted a tractor part where the bent leg had been.
Ava put the colander on top as a brand-new antenna dish.
Grandma Rose sewed a neat patch over a tear in the seat.
Blip pressed the buttons. The ship hummed and lifted off the ground!
It was time to say goodbye. Grandma gave Blip a basket of apples for the trip.
At sunset Blip lifted off, and all the farm animals watched him go.
That night the twins saw a new star blinking at them from the sky.
Far away, Blip munched an apple, blinked his ship's light and said goodnight to his friends.

prompts.name: Tessa and the Mars dust storm

fields.title: Dust Storm on Mars
fields.description: Tessa, twelve, with a shaved head and a patched jumpsuit, is one of the first kids living at Ares Base on Mars. In 24 pages the book shows her days: exercise in low gravity, school over video from Earth, tomatoes in the greenhouse dome, the rover ride to the ice mine, blue Martian sunsets. pageTexts: Tessa is twelve, and she is one of the first kids to live on Mars, at a place called Ares Base.
Every day starts with exercise, because Mars gravity is weak and muscles get lazy fast.
School comes over video from Earth. Messages take up to twenty minutes to arrive, so questions have to wait.
After school Tessa looks after the tomatoes in the greenhouse dome. They are almost ripe.
To go outside, Tessa and Dev suit up in the airlock. The air on Mars is far too thin to breathe.
They ride the six-wheeled rover out to the ice mine with Chief Engineer Okafor.
Ice dug from under the ground gives the base its water and the air everyone breathes.
On Mars the sunsets glow blue. Tessa and Dev never get tired of them.
One evening the weather screen showed a giant dust storm rolling toward the base.
By morning the storm had swallowed the sky. Dust hid the sun completely.
Dust buried the solar farm, and the base's power began to fall.
Without power the greenhouse heaters stopped. Frost crept over the tomato leaves.
The grown-ups were stuck at the ice mine until the storm passed. Someone had to save the greenhouse.
Tessa and Dev knew the path to the solar farm by heart. They made a plan.
They drove the rover into the storm, following the marker poles one by one.
A wheel sank into soft sand. Dev dug it out while Tessa held the lamp.
At the solar farm, only the tops of the panels poked out of the dust.
They brushed and shoveled, panel after panel, while the wind howled.
A cable had snapped. Tessa rerouted it to a spare socket, just like she had practiced.
The lights on the panels blinked on. Power was flowing again!
Back at base the heaters hummed, and the frost melted from the tomatoes.
Days later the dust cleared, and the grown-ups drove home from the ice mine.
Chief Okafor pinned a Storm Crew badge on Tessa and on Dev.
That night the whole base ate the first ripe tomatoes on Mars, and they tasted like home.

pageTexts: Zip is a young comet with a long icy tail, and he is the postman of the solar system.
Every morning he puts on his cap and fills his mailbag with postcards and parcels.
Off he zooms, looping away from the Sun with his tail shining behind him.
First stop is Mercury. Zip drops off a parcel of sun hats at the hot, rocky craters.
Next he visits Earth's Moon and pops a postcard into the crater mailbox.
On Phobos, Mars's tiny lumpy moon, he stops to sort his letters.
He weaves through the asteroid belt, holding his mailbag tight.
On Io, volcanoes puff and bubble. Zip rings the doorbell and hands over a parcel.
On Europa he skates over the cracked ice and slips a letter down to the ocean below.
At Saturn he sits on the rings for lunch and watches the ice drift by.
Under Titan's thick, hazy sky, he leaves a package beside a quiet lake.
On Enceladus, icy geysers shoot into space. Zip holds his mailbag high to keep it dry.
He delivers a postcard to the tallest cliff in the solar system, on Uranus's moon Miranda.
Far out at icy Triton, Neptune's biggest moon, he posts the last letter on his list.
But one letter is left at the bottom of the bag, and it has no address at all.
On the back is a little drawing: a round rock and a dotted path leading past Pluto.
Pluto and its moon Charon point the way. "Out there, past everything," they say.
He flies on into the cold, dark Kuiper Belt, where the Sun looks like a tiny star.
His tail glows like a lantern as he checks rock after rock.
At last he finds a small round rock sitting all alone.
"This is for you," says Zip. The little rock has never had a letter before.
It is a card from the Sun, who can see every rock, even the far-away ones. It says you are not forgotten.
The rock writes a reply straight away, and Zip tucks it into his bag.
Then Zip turns for home, his tail lighting up the dark behind him.

prompts.name: Pickle the porcupine wants a hug

fields.description: A 24-page story. Pickle, a young porcupine with a green scarf, moves to Maple Meadow and wants a friend, but her quills get in the way: she pops the rabbits' balloons, gets stuck in the squirrels' tug-of-war rope and pricks Mole at a picnic. She tries a pillow, a pot and a coat of leaves. Then she rolls up the apples after a windstorm, holds up the frogs' tent in the rain and carries paper lanterns for the meadow party. There an old tortoise gives her the first hug, and everyone else hugs her in oven mitts.

The old tortoise and Pickle in a big hug, his hard shell pressed against her quills, both smiling, a lantern glowing above them.
All the meadow animals wearing oven mitts on their paws in one big group hug around Pickle, lanterns in the trees and a full moon above.
pageTexts: Pickle the porcupine pulled her little wagon into Maple Meadow. "I hope I make a friend here," she said.
Her new home was a cozy burrow under the old oak tree. Pickle unpacked her teacups and wished for someone to share them with.
Over the hedge, the rabbits were having a balloon party. Pickle hurried over to say hello.
She gave the biggest rabbit a hug. Pop! Pop! Pop! Every balloon burst on her quills.
"Sorry," said Pickle, and her nose drooped. The rabbits said it was all right, but the party was very quiet after that.
Next she found the squirrels playing tug-of-war. "I can pull!" said Pickle, and she grabbed the rope.
The rope stuck fast in her quills. The squirrels tumbled into a heap, and nobody could get the rope out.
At the picnic, Pickle sat down close to Mole. "Ouch!" said Mole, and he jumped right off the blanket.
That night Pickle sat alone on a log. "Everyone runs away from my prickles," she sighed.
In the morning she had a plan. She tied her fluffiest pillow onto her back.
But the pillow caught on a bramble and burst. Feathers floated all over the meadow.
Then she tried a big cooking pot. Clank, clonk, clank! It was much too noisy for hugging.
Last she covered her quills with leaves. A deer tried to nibble her, because she looked just like a bush!
Pickle shook off every leaf. "Maybe I can't stop being prickly," she said. "But maybe I can be prickly and kind."
That afternoon a great wind blew through Maple Meadow. Apples tumbled from every tree in the orchard.
Pickle curled up and rolled through the grass. The apples stuck to her quills, ten at a time!
She filled every basket in the meadow. "Thank you, Pickle!" cheered the rabbits and the squirrels.
Then the rain came, and the frogs' tent pole snapped. The wet tent sagged down onto their heads.
Pickle stood up tall in the middle. Her quills held the tent up, and the frogs stayed warm and dry.
Everyone was getting ready for the meadow party. "How will we hang all these lanterns?" asked Mole.
Pickle carried twenty lanterns on her quills at once, and the squirrels hung them on every branch.
At the party, an old tortoise came slowly up to Pickle. "My shell is very hard," he said with a smile.
He gave her a great big hug, and nothing poked at all. It was Pickle's very first hug in Maple Meadow.
Then the rabbits, the squirrels, Mole and the frogs put on oven mitts, and everybody hugged Pickle at once!

pageTexts: On Saturday morning, Amara drew a map of her whole block. There were eight houses on it, and she knew someone in every one.
"Today I'm going to do one kind thing for every house," she told Mom. "Each time I do one, I'll draw a star."
She tucked the map in her pocket and stepped outside. The street was sunny and still a little sleepy.
Next door, Mrs. Kim was looking at six heavy bags of groceries. "I can carry those," said Amara.
They carried every bag up the steps together. Mrs. Kim gave her a clementine, and Amara drew her first star.
Mr. Lopez's back was sore, and his tomatoes were thirsty. Amara watered every plant down the row.
"The best tomato is yours," said Mr. Lopez. Star number two went on the map.
The twins at the yellow house were bored. Amara chalked the longest hopscotch on the whole street.
Soon all three of them were hopping and laughing. The twins added chalk flowers, and Amara added star number three.
Mr. Osei had a broken leg and a puppy who wanted to run. "May I walk him for you?" asked Amara.
Biscuit the puppy pulled her all the way around the block and back again. Star number four!
In the park, Amara spotted a fluffy cat hiding under a bench. It looked just like the picture on the lamppost.
She carried the cat home to the blue house. Its owner hugged it tight, and Amara drew star number five.
At lunch, Amara drew a picture of the mail carrier, who walks their block in sun, rain and snow.
She left it in the mailbox with a thank-you note. When he found it, he smiled all the way down the street. Star six!
In the afternoon, Amara and Mom baked two dozen blueberry muffins. Amara got flour on her nose.
They carried the muffins to the fire station on the corner. "Thank you for keeping our block safe," said Amara.
The firefighters let her sit in the big truck and try on a helmet. Star number seven went on the map.
Her last stop was the senior home at the end of the street. Amara read Mrs. Petrova her favorite book about the sea.
Then Mrs. Petrova taught Amara how to knit one whole row. Star number eight!
As the sun went down, Amara sat on her stoop and looked at her map. Every house had a star.
Then she heard chairs scraping. All her neighbors were carrying tables and food into the street.
"Surprise!" called Mrs. Kim. "You were kind to all of us today, so now it's our turn."
That night Amara drew one more star, the biggest of all, right in the middle of the map, for the whole block.

pageTexts: On Monday, Yusuf came to a new school in a new country. He didn't know a single word of English yet.
The teacher said his name, and the class waved. Yusuf held his cap tight and waved back.
At recess, June sat on the bench. Her arm was in a cast, so she couldn't play tag.
Yusuf sat down at the other end of the bench. Neither of them said anything, because neither knew what to say.
Then Yusuf picked up five smooth stones and set them in a row. He bounced his ball and scooped up a stone before he caught it.
June tried it with her good hand. Bounce, scoop, catch! Yusuf clapped, and June laughed out loud.
On Tuesday, June brought a notebook. She drew a ball, pointed and said, "Ball." Yusuf said, "Ball!"
Yusuf drew a sun and said the word in his language. June tried it, and he grinned at the way she said it.
On Wednesday they learned "lunch," and then they swapped. June loved the flatbread. Yusuf loved the sandwich.
Yusuf drew a girl with pigtails. "Sister," said June, and she drew her baby brother in his high chair.
Then June made her silliest face. "Funny!" she said. Yusuf laughed so hard he nearly fell off the bench.
They made up a secret handshake: a thumb hook, a wiggle and a gentle bump on June's cast.
Yusuf drew a sun and a soccer ball on June's cast. June said it was the best drawing on it.
On Thursday, the class took a bus to the city park. Yusuf and June shared a seat by the window.
They stopped to watch a line of ducklings. When they looked up, the class was gone.
The paths all looked the same. June's tummy went tight, and Yusuf held his ball close.
June opened the notebook and drew the bus beside the big fountain. Yusuf nodded and pointed at the sun.
They walked toward the sun, past the roses and around the hedges, checking June's map as they went.
There was the fountain, and there was their teacher running to meet them. "You found your way back!" she said.
On the bus home they were so tired they fell asleep, still holding the notebook and the ball.
On Friday, the teacher asked if they had something to share. Yusuf and June looked at each other and nodded.
At recess, Yusuf showed everyone the stone game, and June showed them how to play it with just one hand.
Soon the whole playground was bouncing and scooping. Even the tag players wanted a turn.
At the end of the day, Yusuf said his first English sentence: "June is my friend." June said it back in his language.

pageTexts: Puff was a little round cloud with a curl on top. One summer morning, she woke up over a sunny valley.
It was a very hot day. The sun shone and shone, and everything in the valley felt thirsty.
A tired cow was lying in the hot field. Puff floated over her and made a big, cool shadow.
"Moo, thank you!" said the cow, and she munched her grass in the shade.
Next Puff saw a vegetable garden. The carrots and cabbages were droopy and dry.
Puff rained a gentle rain, pitter-patter. The cabbages perked right up. Puff got a little bit smaller.
In the town, a little dog was panting on the hot sidewalk. His water bowl was empty.
Puff sprinkled cool drops on his back and filled his bowl to the top. The little dog wagged and wagged.
Three little birds sat on an empty bird bath. "No splashing today," they peeped.
Puff filled it to the brim. Splish, splash! The birds had the best bath ever. Puff got smaller again.
Over the hill was a field of sunflowers with their big heads hanging low.
Puff rained and rained until every sunflower stood up tall and turned its face to the sky.
Down below, the wind blew the farmer's bonfire toward his haystack. His little bucket was not enough.
Puff squeezed out a big shower. Whoosh! The fire went out in a puff of steam, and the farmer cheered.
Now Puff was not round at all. She was just a tiny wisp floating over the lake.
"I gave all my rain away," she whispered. "Now I'm too small to help anyone."
But the lake had been watching. It breathed up soft, curly mist, all the way to Puff.
The mist joined Puff, and she grew rounder and rounder. Her curl popped back up on top.
Then the wind came whistling over the hills. "Puff! I brought your friends!" it called.
Big clouds and little clouds floated in to meet her, long ones and tall ones and bumpy ones.
Together they made one big, fluffy cloud family, and Puff was the biggest she had ever been.
They rained a soft, happy rain over the whole valley, on the cow, the garden and the sunflowers.
Then the sun peeked out from behind Puff, and its light sparkled in every raindrop.
A great big rainbow stretched across the valley. "Thank you, Puff!" called everyone she had helped.

pageTexts: Maya and Dev were both sure they were the best at science in Room 12. They had never agreed on anything.
Then Ms. Okafor drew names for science fair partners. "Maya and Dev," she read. Both of them groaned.
Maya wanted to test which paper towel was strongest. Dev wanted to build a robot out of an old toaster.
They argued until neither of them had anything left to say. That was when they noticed the chocolate bar melting in the window.
"A solar oven," they said at the exact same time. It was the first thing they had ever agreed on.
They set up a workshop in Dev's garage. Maya made a six-week plan, and Dev collected boxes, foil and an old window.
Version one went together in an afternoon: a pizza box, foil flaps, black paper and plastic wrap on top.
It got hot, all right. The plastic wrap melted into goo, and so did the crayon they used to test it.
Version two got even hotter. A cardboard flap began to smoke, and Maya's dad came running with the hose.
They sat on the step with a soggy, scorched box. "Note: cardboard burns," Maya wrote, and Dev laughed so hard he snorted.
Version three had a wooden crate, the old window for a lid and mirror tiles Dev found at a yard sale.
That night a storm blew in. The wind tore a sheet of roof right off Dev's garage.
In the morning they helped Dev's grandpa fix the roof. Under its tarp, the oven didn't have a scratch.
Maya worked out the sun's angle, and Dev tilted every mirror to match. Teamwork, it turned out, worked.
The thermometer climbed and climbed. "It's working!" yelled Dev, and Maya did a dance on the driveway.
First test: cookies. Maya timed them to the second, and Dev waited with an oven mitt on each hand.
Second test: s'mores. The marshmallows puffed up like clouds, and Dev's little sister ate four.
Third test: a whole pizza. Maya wrote every number in her chart. Dev called it delicious data.
They built their display board on Maya's living room floor, with photos of every oven, even the burned one.
On fair morning, Dev's bike chain snapped halfway to school, with the oven in the trailer behind him.
Maya ran six blocks with her brother's wagon. They loaded the oven and raced to school together.
They made it with two minutes to spare. Maya explained the numbers, Dev explained the build, and the judges ate pizza.
They won honorable mention. Maya and Dev held the ribbon together, and neither one let go first.
On the bus home, Maya turned to a fresh page. "Next year," said Dev, "a wind turbine." Maya was already making a list.

pageTexts: Behind the kitchen wall of the Baker family's house lived a tiny mouse named Nutmeg.
Nutmeg had a matchbox bed, a button rug and a red knitted hat that kept her ears warm.
One snowy December day, the Bakers carried a big Christmas tree into the house.
That night, when everyone was asleep, Nutmeg crept out. "I will make Christmas too," she whispered.
She found a bowl of cranberries on the counter and rolled out one, two, three.
She threaded them on a long string and hung them along the shelf like a necklace.
She hung a shiny thimble from a hook. Ting! It was her very own Christmas bell.
Beside the cookie rack lay crumbs of gingerbread. Nutmeg had a wonderful idea.
She built a little gingerbread cottage with a frosting roof and a chocolate chip door.
She wrapped a walnut in a scrap of paper and tied it with a ribbon. A present!
From an old lost sock, she sewed a little stocking, stitch by tiny stitch.
Then Nutmeg tiptoed into the living room. The tree was so tall and sparkly!
She hopped onto the toy train. Choo choo! Around and around the tree she went.
She sat in a spoon and slid all the way down the banister. Wheee!
Bump! She landed at the bottom of the stairs. The cat opened one eye.
Nutmeg dived into a fluffy slipper and kept very, very still.
The cat yawned and went back to sleep. Phew! Nutmeg crept out of the slipper.
On Christmas Eve, she hung her little stocking by her mouse hole and put the walnut present beside it.
Then she climbed into her matchbox bed and fell fast asleep.
On Christmas morning, the Baker children ran into the kitchen. "Look! Who did all this?"
By the mouse hole they found a tiny stocking, a gingerbread cottage and a walnut wrapped with a bow.
"A mouse made Christmas for us," said the little boy. They put a crumb of cake in the stocking.
When Nutmeg peeked out, she found the cake in her stocking. She hugged it tight.
"Merry Christmas," whispered Nutmeg, and the Baker children waved back.

pageTexts: Thistle was a young reindeer with one crooked antler, and she dreamed of pulling the Christmas sleigh.
In November she lined up at the North Pole Flight School with all the other young reindeer.
Coach Birch looked at her bent antler. "Hmm," he said. "We'll see what you can do."
First came take-off practice on the ice runway. Thistle slipped and slid and spun around.
When she finally lifted off, her crooked antler tipped her sideways.
Crash! She landed in the snowman orchard and knocked the head off a snowman.
The elves put the snowman's head back on. "Try again tomorrow," they told her.
So Thistle practised every morning before anyone else was awake.
In loop class the big reindeer flew perfect circles over the elf village. Thistle flew a wobbly squiggle.
She ended up tangled in a string of Christmas lights between two rooftops.
Then came night flying. Each reindeer carried a lantern through the dark sky.
Thistle's lantern swung, and she lost the line behind a cloud.
A snowy owl flew beside her. "Follow the workshop lights," it hooted, and she found her way back.
At rooftop landing practice, Thistle skidded across the workshop roof and bumped the chimney.
In the harness relay against the older reindeer, Thistle pulled hard, but she finished last again.
That night Thistle lay in the barn. "Maybe a crooked antler can't pull a sleigh," she sighed.
The old sleigh driver, Grandmother Juniper, came by with a lantern. "Don't give up yet, little one," she said.
On Christmas Eve the sleigh was packed, but a howling blizzard swept over the North Pole.
The big reindeer tried to fly, but the wind pushed them back down. "We're grounded," said Coach Birch.
Thistle stepped into the storm. Her crooked antler caught the wind just right, and she rose straight up.
"Put her at the front!" cried Grandmother Juniper. Thistle led the team up through the snow.
Above the clouds the sky was calm and full of stars. They delivered every present before dawn.

fields.description: A 24-page Christmas story. Wilbur, a penguin postmaster in a blue cap, runs the North Pole Post Office. pageTexts: Wilbur the penguin was the postmaster of the North Pole Post Office, and December was his busiest month.
Letters came by plane, dropped from the sky in big canvas bags.
Letters came by boat, handed up the icy dock by a walrus sailor.
And letters came by sled, piled higher than the dogs pulling them.
Wilbur sorted them into mountains: tall ones, short ones, and wobbly ones that fell right over.
Stamp, stamp, stamp! He stamped every single one.
Then the elves loaded the letters onto carts and rolled them off to the workshop.
On December 23, Wilbur was sweeping up when he spotted one letter hiding behind an old mailbag.
It was from a girl named Hana. "Please find my grandpa's lost music box," it said. "It played his favourite song."
The sleigh would leave tomorrow night. There was no time to lose!
Wilbur hitched up the dog sled, tucked the letter in his satchel and set off.
They raced across an iced-over lake, the ice creaking under the runners.
When it grew dark, they stopped at a lighthouse. The keeper lent Wilbur a lantern.
With the lantern swinging, Wilbur followed the path through the snowy forest.
At last he reached a tiny toy-repair shop at the edge of a sleepy village.
The old toymaker read the letter. "People bring me lost toys all year," she said. "Let's look."
They searched shelves of teddy bears, tin drums and wooden horses.
On the very top shelf, Wilbur found a little wooden music box with a dancer on the lid.
The toymaker fixed its spring and wound the key, and a sweet old song tinkled out.
Wilbur raced home all day on Christmas Eve, the music box wrapped safely in his scarf.
He reached the workshop just as the sleigh began to rise. "Wait!" he shouted. "One more!"
An elf leaned over the side and caught the music box. The sleigh flew off into the night.
On Christmas morning, Hana gave the music box to her grandpa. He wound it, and his old song played again.
A week later, a new letter arrived at the post office. It was a thank-you note, with a drawing of a penguin.

pageTexts: On Christmas Eve, Sofia and Max rolled the biggest snowball they had ever made.
They stacked one, two, three snowballs to make a snowman.
Sofia gave him a carrot nose. Max gave him pebble eyes and two stick arms.
Then they put an old captain's cap on his head. "You are Captain Carrot!" they cheered.
That night the children went to bed and waved goodnight to Captain Carrot.
When the house was dark, Captain Carrot blinked his pebble eyes and stretched. He was awake!
He hopped out of the gate and down the snowy street.
At the pond, he skated round and round on the ice. Swish, swoosh!
He found the Christmas market, full of little wooden stalls and twinkly lights.
He rode a painted horse on the carousel, up and down and round and round.
He sang with the carolers under the street lamp. La la la!
The baker had pies to deliver, so Captain Carrot helped carry them.
He left a warm pie on every doorstep on the street.
Up in the tower, he pulled the rope and rang the big bell. Dong, dong!
At the station, he waved at the late train as it puffed by. Toot toot!
He zoomed down the big hill on a tea tray. Wheee!
Then he sat under the big town tree and looked up at the shining star.
The baker wrapped a warm new scarf around his neck. "Thank you for helping," she said.
A stall keeper gave him a candy cane, the biggest one in the whole market.
The sky began to turn pink. "Time to go home!" said Captain Carrot, and he hurried back.
He hopped back into the yard, stood very still, and closed his pebble eyes.
On Christmas morning, Sofia and Max woke up and ran outside in their pajamas and boots.
Captain Carrot had a new scarf and a candy cane! And there were snowy footprints by the gate.
"Merry Christmas, Captain Carrot!" they said. And they were sure he winked.
