pageTexts: Every December, Hattie helped Grandpa at Pine Hollow, the family Christmas tree farm.
One week before Christmas, Grandpa slipped on the icy barn steps.
His arm was broken. "You know this farm better than anyone," he said, and handed Hattie the keys.
At dawn the next day, Hattie pulled on her work gloves. The first cars were already pulling in.
She walked families through the rows and tied a tag to every tree they chose.
She drove the tractor and pulled the hay wagon full of families up and down the hill.
"Will it fit in our living room?" a dad asked. Hattie measured it with the tall pole.
She tied trees to car roofs, pulling the twine tight with the knot Grandpa had taught her.
She kept the bonfire burning so people could warm their hands and toast marshmallows.
At the cocoa stand, she poured mug after mug, with a candy cane in each.
That night she fell asleep at the kitchen table. Grandpa laid a quilt over her with his good arm.
On the third day, a little boy came running. "Our dog Pepper ran into the trees!"
Hattie followed the paw prints deep into the oldest pines.
She found Pepper tangled in a roll of old tree netting, shivering but safe.
She carried Pepper back, and the boy hugged him so hard his hat fell off.
Then the tree baler jammed, with a big fir stuck halfway through and a line of customers waiting.
Grandpa couldn't use his arm, so he talked her through the repair while she worked with the wrench.
With one last turn, the gear clicked into place, and the tree slid out wrapped and ready.
In the evenings she made wreaths in the barn, with pine branches, pinecones and red bows.
On Christmas Eve, Hattie and Grandpa picked the finest tree on the farm. It was not for sale.
They drove it to the children's hospital in town as a gift, with a stack of wreaths beside it.
The children helped decorate it, hanging paper stars and ornaments on every branch.
Back home, there was one small tree left on the hill. They cut it last, just for themselves.
That night their own tree glowed in the farmhouse window. "Best week ever," said Grandpa.

fields.description: Bubbles, a baby seahorse with a curly tail, drifts away from her dad in a strong current on the coral reef. pageTexts: Bubbles was a baby seahorse. She lived on the coral reef with her dad.
One day a big current came. Whoosh! It pulled Bubbles away.
Bubbles looked around. She could not see her dad anywhere.
"Have you seen my dad?" Bubbles asked a clownfish.
"Not today," said the clownfish. "Ask the turtle on the ledge."
The sea turtle was fast asleep. Bubbles gave his shell a tap.
"Mmm, try past the sand," yawned the turtle.
Past the sand was a pufferfish. "Go away!" he puffed.
Then he felt sorry. "Ask the eel in the rocks," he said.
The moray eel opened his big mouth. "Ask the shrimp," he said.
The shrimp were busy cleaning a grouper's teeth.
"Go that way," they said, and pointed with their feelers.
That way was an octopus who could change her stripes to spots!
"Hold on," said the octopus, and lifted Bubbles over the wall.
Crunch, crunch! A parrotfish was eating coral.
"I make sand," said the parrotfish. "Follow it to the ray."
The ray let Bubbles ride along. Swoosh, over the sand!
"Your dad likes the seagrass," said the ray. "It is just there."
Bubbles was very tired. But she did not give up.
She came to the seagrass meadow. The grass was so tall!
Bubbles swam between the blades. "Dad? Dad!"
And there was Dad, holding onto the grass, waiting for her.
Bubbles curled her tail around his. "I found you!"
All her new friends came to say hello. Bubbles was home.

pageTexts: Juno was born in a warm blue lagoon. Her mother pushed her up gently for her very first breath.
Juno had one white flipper. She liked to rest under her mother's big flipper and drink milk.
Every day she practised jumping. Her first breach was more of a flop, but she was proud.
When spring came, her mother said, "Now we swim north, all the way to the cold seas."
Spinner dolphins joined them on the first day. They spun in the air and dared Juno to race.
At night they rested over a coral bank, where turtles and little fish swam below.
Juno learned to breathe in rhythm with her mother: swim, swim, up, puff.
A giant ship rumbled past. "Ships are loud," said her mother. "We stay well away."
One morning, tall black fins appeared. Orcas! Juno hid beneath her mother.
Her mother lifted her mighty tail and stood her ground. The orcas swam away.
Farther north, sea lions barked at Juno from a buoy. She barked a bubble right back.
They swam deep under a fishing boat. "Never play near the nets," her mother warned.
Along the coast was a kelp forest, where a sea otter cracked open his lunch.
Juno poked her head straight up to look at the land. A lighthouse looked back.
That evening, she heard a strange, beautiful sound. Far away, other whales were singing.
Juno tried to sing too. It came out squeaky, but her mother said it was perfect.
Then a storm came. The waves were as tall as hills, but Juno stayed close and kept swimming.
When the storm was over, a rainbow stretched across the sky, and Juno slapped the water for joy.
Day after day they crossed the open ocean. Flying fish skipped ahead like a welcome.
At last the water turned icy. Juno saw her first iceberg, with a puffin on top.
The sea was full of krill, tiny shrimp by the million. This was why they had come!
The grown whales swam in a circle and blew a net of bubbles to round up the krill.
Juno blew bubbles too. Then everyone rose up together, mouths wide, for a giant gulp.
Full and happy, Juno rested beside her mother. She had swum the whole way north.

prompts.name: Finn's message in a bottle

fields.title: Finn and the Bottle Message
fields.description: Finn, eight, in a striped life jacket, finds a bottle on the beach with a hand-drawn picture map inside. He and his grandpa sail their small boat, the Pelican, to follow it. They stop at a lighthouse island, a sandbar full of seals, a mangrove with a heron's nest, a reef they snorkel over, a cove with a shipwreck and a fishing village where an old woman recognizes the map: she drew it as a girl seventy years ago. The last mark leads to a tin of her childhood treasures buried under a palm. Finn adds his own drawing and they bury it again. 24 pages.

prompts.why: Parents and grandparents get a 24-page sea adventure with islands, boats and a treasure hunt, and no pirates.
prompts.pageStyle: Black-and-white story coloring page for a child aged 6 to 9. Finn, eight, has messy hair, a striped life jacket, shorts and sandals; Grandpa is tall, with a white beard, a knitted cap and rolled sleeves; the Pelican is a small one-sail boat. Medium outlines, moderate detail and background, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.

Finn carrying a picnic basket along a wooden dock while Grandpa coils a rope on the deck of the Pelican, a life ring hanging on a post.
The Pelican sailing out of the harbor with its sail full of wind, Finn at the front holding the map up, a gull following the boat.
Finn and Grandpa tying up at a rocky jetty below a tall striped lighthouse, Finn pointing from the map to the lighthouse with a grin.
Finn at the top of the lighthouse looking through a brass spyglass over the railing, a long sandbar out at sea far below.
Grandpa rowing a little dinghy toward a sandbar covered in lounging seals, a seal pup flopping down to the water's edge to look at Finn.
Finn sitting in the dinghy checking the map, finger on the bird-in-a-tree drawing, while two seals lift their heads to watch him.
The dinghy slipping between the twisting roots of a mangrove, small crabs clinging to the roots and leaves arching overhead.
A heron standing guard beside its stick nest of fuzzy chicks high in the mangrove branches, Finn watching quietly through binoculars.
Finn and Grandpa eating sandwiches on the deck of the anchored Pelican, Grandpa pointing to the fish drawing on the map with a crust.
Finn snorkeling over a coral reef in a mask and flippers, angelfish and a brain coral below him, the Pelican's hull floating above.
Finn floating face down beside a sea turtle swimming past a giant clam with its wavy shell open on the reef.
A quiet cove with an old wooden shipwreck tilted on the sand, its curved ribs showing, crabs on the planks and the Pelican anchored outside.
Finn climbing carefully inside the shipwreck, running his hand over a small star carved into an old beam, Grandpa holding up a lantern.
Finn and Grandpa walking up the dock of a fishing village with houses on stilts, fishing nets hung up to dry and small boats pulled onto the sand.
An old woman with a grey bun and a shawl mending a fishing net on her porch, Finn holding the map out toward her.
The old woman holding the map in both hands, one hand on her cheek in surprise, Finn and Grandpa leaning in close.
The old woman's kitchen: she shows Finn an old notebook of drawings in the same style as the map, a cat on the windowsill and glasses of lemonade on the table.
Finn, Grandpa and the old woman walking along a sandy path to a tall leaning palm on a point of land, Finn carrying a small shovel.
Finn digging between the roots of the palm tree, a rusty tin box poking out of the sand, the old woman clapping her hands.
The open tin: glass marbles, a seashell necklace, a small carved wooden boat and a ribbon, the old woman smiling as she holds up the boat.
Finn putting his own folded drawing into the tin as Grandpa pats the sand back down under the palm, the sun setting over the sea.
pageTexts: Finn was hunting for shells at low tide when he saw something shining in the sand. A bottle!
Inside was a rolled-up paper. "Grandpa!" Finn shouted. "Come and look!"
It was a map with no words, just little pictures joined by a dotted line. "Let's follow it," said Grandpa.
The next morning they packed a picnic and got the Pelican ready to sail.
Out of the harbor they went, with the wind in the sail and the map in Finn's hand.
The first picture was a lighthouse. And there it was, on a rocky little island!
From the top, Finn could see far out to sea. "I see a sandbar next!"
The sandbar was covered in seals. One curious pup came to say hello.
Finn checked the map. The next picture was a bird in a tree.
They rowed into a mangrove, where the roots twisted like fingers into the water.
High in the branches was a heron on her nest. "Bird in a tree," Finn whispered.
Over lunch, Grandpa tapped the map. "A fish next. Time to get wet."
Finn snorkeled over the reef. Fish of every shape swam around him.
A sea turtle glided by, and a giant clam opened its wavy shell.
The next picture was a boat. In a quiet cove lay an old shipwreck.
Inside, carved into a beam, was a little star, just like the one on the map.
The dotted line ended at a village. "Someone here must know this map," said Grandpa.
Finn showed the map to an old woman mending her nets on the porch.
Her eyes went wide. "I drew this when I was a girl," she said, "seventy years ago!"
She showed them her old notebook. The drawings looked just the same.
"The last picture is my secret palm tree," she said. "Let's go and see."
Finn dug and dug under the palm. Clink! His shovel hit a rusty tin.
Inside were her childhood treasures. She laughed and held up her little wooden boat.
Finn added a drawing of his own, and they buried the tin again for someone new to find.

prompts.name: Amaya's dive to the ocean floor

fields.title: Down to the Abyss
fields.description: Amaya, twelve, with a braid tucked into a ship's cap, joins her mother's research crew for a dive in the submersible Kestrel. They sink through the zones: the sunlit zone with tuna and jellyfish, the twilight zone with lanternfish and a giant squid's eye in the dark, the midnight zone with an anglerfish and a vampire squid, then the abyss with sea pigs and glass sponges. At the bottom they reach a hydrothermal vent with tube worms and white crabs, and Amaya spots a sea cucumber no one has seen before. Back on deck, the scientists name the new species after her. 24 pages.

prompts.why: Older ocean fans and science teachers get a 24-page dive through every ocean zone with real deep-sea animals at each depth.
prompts.pageStyle: Black-and-white story coloring page for ages 9 to 13. Amaya, twelve, has a braid tucked into a ship's cap and a pocketed jacket; her mother has short curly hair and a headset; the Kestrel is a round submarine with a dome window, two robot arms and lamps. Fine detailed lines, full backgrounds, no shading or grey, no words in the picture, a blank band at the bottom for text, portrait 8.5 x 11 page.
pages: A research ship on a calm sea at dawn, its crane swinging the round submersible Kestrel over the side, Amaya at the rail with her sketchbook under one arm.
Amaya climbing down the hatch on top of the Kestrel, her mother already inside, deck crew in hard hats and life vests holding the cables.
Inside the Kestrel: three seats facing a big round window, screens and dials, a pilot at the joystick and Amaya pressing her hands to the glass.
The Kestrel splashing down into the waves, two divers in wetsuits unhooking it from the crane line, the ship's hull towering beside it.
The sunlit zone through the dome window: a school of fast tuna streaking past, beams of sunlight slanting down through the water.
Moon jellyfish drifting past the Kestrel's window with long trailing arms, a sea turtle far off, the sunbeams fading above.
The twilight zone: a school of small lanternfish dotted with rows of glowing spots, swimming in the dim water around the submersible's lamps.
A giant squid's enormous eye at the very edge of the Kestrel's lamplight, long tentacles trailing into the dark, Amaya gasping at the window.
Amaya inside the cabin sketching a hatchetfish in her book, her mother writing notes beside her, a depth gauge and a thermos on the panel.
The midnight zone: an anglerfish with a glowing lure dangling in front of its wide, toothy mouth, lit up by the submersible's lamps.
A vampire squid turning its webbed arms inside out over its body like a spiky cloak, two big eyes staring at the window.
A gulper eel with a huge balloon-like mouth and a long whip tail, a few comb jellies with rippling stripes drifting nearby.
A small dumbo octopus flapping its ear-like fins as it hovers in the dark water in front of the Kestrel's lamps.
The abyss: the Kestrel's lights shining on a soft muddy seafloor where a group of sea pigs walk along on tiny tube feet.
Tall glass sponges shaped like lacy vases on the seafloor, a brittle star curled on one, a tripod fish standing on its long fin spikes.
One of the Kestrel's robot arms pushing a clear tube into the mud to take a sample, Amaya and her mother working the controls together.
A hydrothermal vent: a tall rocky black chimney on the seafloor puffing thick clouds of hot mineral smoke into the water.
Thick bundles of giant tube worms with feathery tips around the vent, white crabs crawling over the rocks between them.
A strange see-through sea cucumber with frilly lace fins floating above the seafloor, Amaya pointing at it through the dome window.
The robot arm gently scooping the new sea cucumber into a clear collection box, the pilot steering, Amaya watching with both hands clasped.
The Kestrel rising toward the surface after dropping its ballast weights, a trail of bubbles streaming up from it in the dark water.
The Kestrel bobbing at the surface at sunset, divers reattaching the crane line, the research ship waiting close by.
Scientists in the ship's lab crowding around a glass tank holding the sea cucumber, Amaya at the front with her sketchbook open.
The crew clapping as a scientist pins Amaya's drawing of the new sea cucumber on the lab wall, her mother hugging her from the side.
pageTexts: At dawn the crane lifted the Kestrel over the side of the ship. Amaya had waited her whole life for this dive.
Her mother was the lead scientist, and today Amaya was part of the crew. She climbed down the hatch and the lid sealed shut above her.
Inside, there were three seats, a hundred dials and one big round window. Amaya pressed her hands against the cold glass.
With a splash the Kestrel hit the water. The divers unhooked the line, and they began to sink.
The first part of the ocean is the sunlit zone. Tuna flashed past like silver arrows in the sunbeams.
Moon jellyfish drifted by. Above them, the light was already fading from blue to grey.
At two hundred meters they entered the twilight zone. Lanternfish twinkled like a sky full of stars.
Then something huge moved at the edge of the lights: the eye of a giant squid, bigger than a dinner plate. It blinked, and was gone.
Amaya sketched every animal she saw. Her mother logged the depth: five hundred meters and falling.
Below a thousand meters, no sunlight ever reaches. In the midnight zone, an anglerfish dangled its glowing lure.
A vampire squid flipped its arms over its head like a cloak. It looked fierce, but it was only shy.
A gulper eel opened a mouth far too big for its body. Comb jellies rippled with light around it.
Then came Amaya's favorite: a tiny dumbo octopus, flapping its fins like little ears.
After three hours they reached the abyss, four thousand meters down. Sea pigs plodded across the mud.
Glass sponges stood like delicate vases, and a tripod fish waited patiently on its three long fins.
"Your turn," said her mother. Amaya steered the robot arm and took her first mud sample.
Farther on, the water grew warm. Ahead stood a hydrothermal vent, puffing black smoke from inside the Earth.
Giant tube worms crowded around it, and white crabs scuttled between them. Life, even here, in the dark.
Then Amaya saw something no one on board had seen before: a see-through sea cucumber with frilly fins.
Very gently, the robot arm guided it into a collection box. Amaya held her breath the whole time.
The Kestrel dropped its weights and began the long climb back toward the light.
When they reached the surface, the sun was setting. The divers were waiting to bring them home.
In the lab, the scientists crowded around the tank. Nobody could find the creature in any book.
"Every new species needs a name," said her mother. They named it after Amaya, and pinned her drawing on the wall.

prompts.name: Pearl the hermit crab's new shell

fields.title: Pearl Needs a New Shell
fields.description: Pearl, a hermit crab with striped legs and one big claw, has grown too big for her snail shell. She sets off across the tide pools to find a new home. She tries a bottle cap, a teacup washed up on the sand, a toy bucket, a coconut, an old boot, a sea urchin's empty shell and a jar, and every one is too big, too small, too heavy or too leaky. She asks a starfish, a sea anemone, a gull and a lobster for help. At the edge of the rocks she finds a whelk shell that fits just right, and she gives her old shell to a smaller crab. 24 pages.

prompts.why: Parents of toddlers get a funny 24-page tide pool story where every page is one more shell to try.

A big lobster under a rock ledge with long feelers and huge claws, Pearl standing in front of it, looking tiny.
The lobster pointing one huge claw toward the far edge of the rocks, Pearl turning to look with her eyes stretched up on their stalks.

pageTexts: Pearl the hermit crab had a problem. Her shell was too small!
She squeezed and she squished. But her big claw would not fit inside.
"I need a new home," said Pearl, and off she went.
She found a bottle cap. Too small!
She found a teacup. Too big! Pearl slid all around.
She found a toy bucket. Way too big!
"Can you help me?" she asked a starfish. "Keep looking," said the starfish.
She found a coconut. Too heavy! It would not move.
She found an old boot. Too leaky! Drip, drip, drip.
"Can you help me?" she asked a sea anemone. "Not me," it said, and waved.
She found a sea urchin shell. Too many holes!
"Can you help me?" she asked a gull. "Squawk!" said the gull.
She found a jar. Too slippery! And everyone could see in.
Pearl sat down. "Nothing is right," she said with a sigh.
Then she met a big lobster. "Can you help me?" she asked.
"Go to the edge of the rocks," said the lobster.
So Pearl walked and walked to the very edge of the rocks.
And there it was: a tall, pointy shell.
She peeked inside. Nobody home!
Quick as a wink, Pearl wiggled in.
It fit just right! Pearl did a happy dance.
Then she saw a tiny crab with no shell at all.
"Here," said Pearl. "You can have my old one."
Now they both had homes, and they waved to all their friends.
